utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, your concerns are now satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to thank my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're having technical difficulties, perhaps I can say -- ask a question before we proceed, and that has to do with the exhibits that are going to be tendered in conjunction with this statement, and it's unclear to us how that's going to be identified in the record. Which exhibits from the Brdjanin transcript are actually on the 65 ter list and the cross-reference to the exhibit number in the Brdjanin and the exhibit number in our case. Because we're going to be reading the Brdjanin transcript that has an exhibit number, P1; that same document may be P50 in our case. And without a cross-reference you can't read and understand the Brdjanin transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought we dealt with this last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the Registry will assume the responsibility of sub-numbering the exhibits. Whatever number they would have had before in the previous trial would fall away, and that would be provided to the parties as soon as -- as soon as that exercise is complete. Does that answer your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are the microphone problems solved, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I think they are. I think you can hear me clearly now. Very well. I want to show the witness some photographs if Your Honours please, that are already on our 65 ter list. Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 2145.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Karabeg, do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: These are stalls at Manjaca where we were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender that photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P55, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. The next photo I'd like the witness to be shown is 65 ter 2146.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about those buildings? Do you recognise those buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, what are they?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: These are also the stalls -- or, rather, stables at Manjaca. And most probably these are the three stables in the second camp where they -- we were, and I was in this one in the centre, in the stable in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those three buildings used to accommodate prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tendered, admitted, and marked with the next number in the series.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P56, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you for that. And may the witness be shown 64 -- 65 ter 2144. Could we have it just a bit bigger if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not so much interested in the people who you can see in the photograph unless, of course, you happen to recognise any one individual. But in particular, do you recognise the buildings and structures that you can see in the background?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do recognise them. On the right-hand side is another stable; it's also a stable. And the roof that we see there, that was the kitchen where the food was prepared and where we got our food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the kitchen was out in the open, was it, just covered by that roof?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tendered, admitted, and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P57, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2143.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, forgetting the individuals you see in that particular photograph and looking at the interior of that building, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is the interior of a stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: At Manjaca, yes. The same stables that we've been shown before. And I apologise for one thing. We camp inmates do not refer to this as premises. We call them stables because they were stables, and they were used for keeping cattle in before we were arrested and brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In your time at Manjaca did you ever see prisoners assembled in that fashion, that is, gathered along in a corridor, so to speak, leading alongside the fences, the iron fences, with their shoes neatly arranged in front of them and sitting down in that fashion? Did you ever see that sort of collection of prisoners in that -- in that manner of gathering?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Here in this stable there were three rows. Here we have the central row and then to the left and the right we all sat there arranged like this. We were in two rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How and when did this arrangement occur?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I really can't tell you because I arrived at Manjaca on the 28th of May -- on the 28th of August, 1992, and this camp had become operational or had been opened in early June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were at Manjaca, did you ever see the prisoners collected in that fashion as depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was done as ordered by those who actually were in charge of Manjaca. These were policemen and soldiers. We referred to them as the motley group because they had on camouflage uniforms, multicoloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And just tell the Trial Chamber, if you can, was this the common way for prisoners to be assembled inside these stables, or was this a fairly unusual method of assembling them?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This was the common way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P58, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2255. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you recognise that structure there with the red-painted apparently steel doors.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And tell the Trial Chamber what that place is.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is a camp, a concrete camp, in Sanski Most where I was detained also, in the third garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you use the word "garage." What sort of garage was it? Was it used to keep motor vehicles in there prior to the war, or was it used for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it was used for motor vehicles before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And I seek to tender that photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P59, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. And I would now like to show the witness 65 ter 2422. And in particular, I would like to show the witness page 41 of the B/C/S version, and the translation appears at page 38 of the English. I don't think that we've got the right English. Certainly the B/C/S is correct, and it's the correct page as well. Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please. No. No. The -- the B/C/S version, I understand, had an entry that I was interested in at 0037-9462. That was the ERN.

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a quick intervention before the -- just for the record, this document was not noted in the list to be used in direct examination that was provided to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we're about to take a break now, and perhaps the -- Mr. Di Fazio can get that sorted out in the interim. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Karabeg, I should say, you were asked questions about the document, part of which is in front of you on the screen, in the Brdjanin case, and you were asked about a number of entries in that -- in this document. I just want to direct your attention to the entry that you see in front of you, and I want you to look in particular at item 4. Can you -- can you see that clearly or not? We can possibly enlarge it a little bit further for you. Perhaps I can hasten things by just reading it and then ask you a question. Item 4 says: "Take into custody ..." And then a number of names follow. In your testimony you said -- MR. DI FAZIO: And for the parties they'll find this at T -- or transcript 6139, 6139.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In your testimony you said you were arrested on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This item 4 says: "Take into custody..." Various people. And I'll read out their names. And I want I want to know from you is if in the -- at the time of your arrest on the 25th of May, you said you were taken to the police station in Sanski Most, whether you saw any of these people either on the day or in the days following. Adil Draganovic. Did you see that man after your arrest or on the day of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Redzo Kurbegovic? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Stipo Catic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ismet Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Nihad Kljucanin?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I didn't see Nihad that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And what about in the days -- say, the two or three days after your arrest? Did you see him then? And if you didn't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I did. I did. Not on that day, the 25th of May, just that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when did -- approximately when did you see him in relation to the 25th? Was it months later or in the following days?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think it was either Wednesday or Thursday. So that could have been the 28th or the -- actually, the 27th or the 28th of May when he was brought to the cell where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Nedzad Muhic. Did you see him on the day of your arrest or in the days immediately following?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: On the day of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Hasib Kamber?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I saw Hasib Kamber perhaps about a month after that, some 20 days to a month later, since the time that I was arrested on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Ahmet Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I saw Ahmet Paunovic only at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And Hase Osmancevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I saw Hase Osmancevic precisely on the 25th of May. He was arrested on the same day that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And finally, Fikret Saletovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The same, on the 25th of May. I'm not saying 1992 here, because it all took place in 1992. So that is implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that forms part of the 92 ter package of this witness. I don't think I need to seek to tender it into evidence or have it marked for identification at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I think it would make sense to first have the transcripts tendered into evidence and admitted into evidence. And then once we have an exhibit number for each of the transcripts, then we can assign sub-numbers to each of the documents that go with them. So if you would please tender the transcripts as they come. MR. DI FAZIO: Transcripts or documentary exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, the system is that we -- we admit the transcripts as the main exhibit, and if you have two or three transcripts, then we will give them two or three exhibit numbers, one number each. Now, if, in the tail of each of these transcripts a number of documents follow, then they will be given sub-exhibit numbers. So if this document relates to one of the transcripts, then we first give an exhibit number to this transcript, it's going to be P60; and then all the documents that follow in the tail or within the ambit of this transcript will then be given sub-numbers such as 60.1, 6.2, 60.3, and so on. MR. DI FAZIO: That's clear to me. And so therefore that process should be an automatic one in respect of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes except that we haven't given actually exhibit numbers to the main transcripts. So we need those first, and then we will -- MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. Then I would certainly seek to give the transcripts principal exhibit numbers, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then get on with it. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will become P60, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't have any further questions of this witness if Your Honours please. I'll seek to tender this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karabeg. I am Slobodan Cvijetic, co-counsel in the Mico Stanisic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Nice to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have no intention of asking you about what you went through at Betonirka and Manjaca. In any event, we read that in your testimony, and that speaks for itself. And may I just say that nobody would wish anything like that to be repeated to anyone again. What I'm interested in is what happened afterwards when you crossed into the territory of the Bosnian forces. Can you tell us the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think that this was on the 31st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you can perhaps tell us in a couple of sentences how this happened, how you managed to get to the territory under the control of the Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It was like this: While we were in the camp, that day -- I'm not able to be specific about the date. Perhaps it was the 30th or the 31st of October. After breakfast it was announced that an exchange would be effected that day, and one of the inmates told me that I was on that list. Sometime -- actually, I remember that it was a nice day, so at some point about -- well, 61 of us were called out from those two camps. We were taken in front of the building of the camp administration. We were told that we would be exchanged, 61 of us. We went to a bus. There were four guards. But we inmates, as we were watching the buses passing by, because each bus had to pass by the camp, we would be watching if the inmates were sitting normally and looking through the windows or if their heads were bent forward. There were four guards. There was half a bus, and then immediately they started beating us, and they said, Nobody should raise their head. You need to keep your heads down. This was half way along the route which went through Mrkonjic and Jajce and over Mount Vlasic, via Travnik, up to Turbe. That is where we waited, actually at Mount Vlasic, because there was some complications in this exchange. Then there were these two men who were wearing precisely Chetniks uniforms, with beards, and they had ammunition cross-belts and weapons, large knives, and they asked the guard who had brought us in the bus to give them two of us so that they could slit our throats. The guard said, What's the matter? Are you crazy? They refused to do that, but this lasted for about two hours, you know. After that, our bus set off. We were brought to Turbe, and we were exchanged in Turbe. I think the Serbs were coming out of one bus. We were coming out of this bus. They went to their territory. We went to our territory. One thing we did notice, and that was that those Serbs who were exchanged, they were all looking well. They were shaved. Their clothes were ironed. We noticed that. Whereas we were all crumpled, dirty, because of the conditions we had been living in. The exchange was completed. We stayed in Turbe, and then from Turbe we were taken to Travnik and we were placed somewhere. I don't know where the people who had been exchanged were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Manjaca camp administration, do you know who the administrator or the warden was? Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: He was a colonel. He was from Montenegro. I didn't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was he a military officer, and did he have that rank?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. He was a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. What we started to talk about, I'm interested in this: Did you begin to participate in the political life in the territory under the control of Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in politics even before I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But -- so was this the case when you came back?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please, because this is cross-examination. My time is limited. So my -- my time is running out. So can you just list these things.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I immediately got involved in establishing the civilian authorities of the War Presidency of the Sanski Most municipality with a provisional seat in Zenica and then in Travnik, because before the war I was the President of the Executive Board of the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would I like Witness -- the witness to be shown 1D00-4515, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, on the left side you can see the version in B/C/S. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, can you perhaps zoom in a little bit? The letters are too small. I cannot see to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber has nothing against that, I have a copy which is -- which has bigger print. Perhaps I can show that to the witness if the Trial Chamber permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document now. It's the second column to the right under number II. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the decision appointing you as vice-president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. So you were the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, from what I understood, this decision replaced an earlier decision on the establishment of the War Presidency. That's what it says on the second page. I'm going to show it later in the final remarks and provisions - we're colleagues, so you know how that goes. Anyway, can you, please, tell us when was the first time that you become a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I became a member of the War Presidency for the first time when it was formed. This was in early 1993, because all these citizens in the municipality of Sanski Most and the refugees had heard that I had been exchanged, and they were waiting for me to become involved as an official representative of the legitimate local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have a couple of these transitional provisions where it says that War Presidency practically replaced the legal and official organs until they are able to convene. Did I understand correctly the essence of the jurisdiction of the War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then the next provision says that War Presidencies are obliged to prepare the terrain for the legal organs of authority on the territory under the control of Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Just one moment. What it said is that they are ready to take over authority once they came to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the end where it says that with this decision the decision on the formation and elections of the War Presidency ceases to be in effect. The earlier decision. So you would agree with me that there was a War Presidency from earlier but that you became a member when it says here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret this provision that it substitutes the previous War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You cannot interpret it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, please observe a small pause between question and answer, because it is impossible for the interpreters to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now? Can you interpret that provision? If you can take a look and read it. What it says there is --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Which provision?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You would have to give this back to me so that I can point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we please get page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It is Roman numerals XX. The two X's there. Can you read that paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It says: "When this decision comes into effect it supersedes the decisions on the election of presidents and members of the Wartime Presidencies of the municipal assemblies." Well, you see, this was in 1993. Some municipalities already had Wartime Presidencies in place, and they had provisional seats in Zenica and Travnik. Some people would leave the Presidency and then they needed -- new members needed to be elected. And here it does not specifically mention Sanski Most. It mentions -- it actually provides for War Presidencies in various municipalities. And this was necessary because a huge number of people had been expelled, and all these people had to be re-elected, and then they had to get to know what it was to do -- they were to do, then once the Presidencies were formed, this was on the territory in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, so you agree with me that there were in some towns there already were War Presidencies but they only had different memberships, if I'm correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it like this. Had I, by any chance, arrived there in July or August 1992, I'm certain that the Sanski Most municipality would have a Wartime Presidency then, and some municipalities already did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the gist of my question. Some municipalities did have War Presidencies in place. That's all I was asking about.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. I will organise my stuff, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, or good evening. My name is Igor Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my colleague, but I failed to submit this document for admittance into evidence. I apologise. If we could just get a number assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D10 under seal -- no, it's not under seal, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are on the same topic, I don't believe that we have exhibit number for Prosecution for OTP document 2422. This is a kind of diary or -- so maybe my colleague Gramsci -- Mr. Di Fazio can clarify that or ... MR. DI FAZIO: We discussed this. It's going to be part of the -- of the 65 ter package as Your Honours made it very clear you will be giving the one exhibit number with sub-numbers, and that will be assigned in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, because maybe it was a bit of confusion, because it was on the list of OTP, but, okay, we can move on. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karabeg, I apologise for these few procedural matters. If I understood you correctly, you are an attorney; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you have your own office, and you're still employed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember -- namely, you gave several statements to the Prosecution, and I have a statement of yours dated July 2nd, 2004. I also have a copy for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here on the second page we can see that this is not really a statement. Rather, it is some clarification that you're making here. Could you please read it to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Do you mean the portion where it says: "On the 29th of May ..." and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, all right. I'll read it to myself. That's why I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the way I understand your statement here is you're saying here that you testified in the Krajisnik case in 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next you say that you were referring to certain notes in your diary in the course of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then you concluded that you were unable to locate those notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this diary that was your personal journal, you had given it to an investigator, Mr. Tollefsen; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that you fled from Sanski Most on the 25th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this. I have the original prepared by this gentleman here, and I know what it says there, and I am sure that this was added here, because I already had a suspicion that this gentleman would abuse or misuse this document. I did not flee Sanski Most on the 25th of May, 1992, and you can see there were exact quotations about Sanski Most, and his conduct was such that it gave rise to my suspicions that he might add something to the notes. It is true that I did write some things and I did provide him with a brief notebook. I don't know what -- what he said who he was. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please, just to consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, sir. But certainly you stand by your statement here that you had fled from Sanski Most on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. How could I have fled when I was actually arrested on the 25th of May, 1992, at 1700 hours -- 1750 hours, and I was taken to the police station in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what you signed, you did not sign true facts in this statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you did sign it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I did not sign the statement in this form. I did sign it, but not in this form, not this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic. You graduated from law school in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What year was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the time, you probably had to take an exam in a curriculum called constitution law; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really don't understand where he's headed with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, counsel's duty is to ask questions according to the instructions of his clients, and unless the Court finds -- unless the Chamber finds it irrelevant, then you're required to answer. So at this point the Chamber's prepared to presume that he has a point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I did. I did have that curriculum. I went and attended the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I -- my dear colleague, I have to ask you a question because I read your -- the transcript from the Brdjanin case, and I know that on that occasion you had some legal discussions with Mr. Ackerman at the time, but you're here a fact witness, so please answer my questions with a yes or no, because the system here is a bit different to the system that is used in Europe. So I am entitled to leading questions during cross-examination. So let's just move on. Now, would you agree with me that during the Tito regime, the so-called Tito regime, the -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was a system in place which provided for so-called equality of all three constituent ethnicities; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. The interpreter is not sure if it's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, unfortunately -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, yes. I've answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your answer is yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. And this is the third or fourth time that I'm repeating it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I heard you very well, colleague, but it was not in the transcript, and it's important that it be there, and that is why I am repeating it. So the constitutional system in Bosnia and Herzegovina had a system which provided for the protection of the vital interests of each of the constitutional ethnicities or nations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this was the case also after the multi-party elections in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't have occasion recently to come across the constitutional provisions, but if I tell you that there was a council for the equality of nations based on the constitutional amendments, you would agree with me, right, that it was in existence during the regime in Bosnia and Herzegovina then; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript. I said the constitutional regime, not regime in Bosnia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And based on the so-called Dayton Constitution, which is now in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is also a system in place that is to provide the vital interests of each of the constituent nations and ethnicities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, through the parliamentary system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like your opinion on something. You've probably heard of Belgium and that there is a system in place there between the Valonians and the Flemish, the so-called alarm-bell system. Are you aware of this? Have you heard of this system?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, well the portion that was towards France and the other one that is here. So the Valonians and the Flemish, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the period prior to 1992, and this should include both the single-party and the multi-party period, would you agree with me that this system of national or ethnic quotas or the distribution of functions between the three different constituent ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was abided by? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. But if you allow me a comment, beginning in November 1943, of course, there were both Croats and Serbs and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So Bosnia and Herzegovina was neither Bosnian nor Croat nor Serbian -- or, rather, it was both Bosnian and Serbian and Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I assume that this practice was in place also in Sanski Most, the practice of respect for each of the three constituent ethnicities or nationalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, up until a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What point?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let's say up until April 1992. And I'm just speaking here of Sanski Most. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm sure that this will all become clear, but it's not clear to me at this stage that the practice that Mr. Pantelic refers to and the witness seems to know what he's talking about is clear to everyone else. The practice of respect, is that a -- is that a reference to an entrenched legal system whereby respect is afforded to the other constituent peoples? Am I correct in understanding the evidence in that fashion? It's not clear to me, and I would like to know exactly with Mr. Pantelic means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Gladly, yes. I will clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's indisputable that the principles of the protection of the vital interests of all the three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina were respected from the top of the pyramid to the base where the municipalities were, if I can put it that way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what you are saying now is that at a certain point, and this is -- let's see what you've said. April 1992. In Sanski Most this system of equality of all three peoples was not respected any more. Is that correct? How did this look in practice in April in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I would like you to ask me how it was up until April, if you wish. I would prefer that. From the -- since the elections up until April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because we don't have much time, you agreed with me that up until April in Sanski Most there was a kind of co-existence among the three peoples; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So this coalition was made up by the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ at the level of Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And by inter-party agreements, you split up the posts according to party quotas?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, not according to the quotas but according to the result of the elections from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. But as of April 1992, according to you, why was this principle no longer respected? Can you please explain that to the Trial Chamber briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: One of the peoples began to arrest, detain, and kill the two other peoples, meaning that the Serbs began to arrest, prosecute, kill non-Serbs, or, namely, Muslims and Croats. This was something that started from April onwards. It was a kind of introduction. From the 3rd of April, I think, 1992, the Serbian Assembly was convened, which, as an illegal organ, declared Sanski Most to be Serbian Sanski Most and that Sanski Most was being joined to the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, dear colleague, that Republika Srpska is a reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: You mean now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean now.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the entire constitutional system is protected by an international contract or the Dayton Accords; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did Muslims kill Serbs in the environs of Sanski Most in that period of April/May 1992? Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Muslims kill Serbs? Because you said that Serbs were killing Muslims and Croats. So I'm putting a simple question to you. Now, a very simple question --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, they did not. No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Croats kill Serbs in the area of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, they did not. We're talking about Sanski Most area now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, did Muslims kill Serbs in the Sanski Most region?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Croats kill Serbs in the Sanski Most area in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to a different topic, and that is, Are you aware of the fact that the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed -- formed after the multi-party elections sometime in late 1991, voted a declaration on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who voted for this declaration?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And which ethnicity were those deputies?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't counting. The deputies voted and adopted that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that while voting for the declaration on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb deputies left the session because this was a violation of their vital right as a constituent people, and if I were to tell you that Muslim and Croat deputies voted on that declaration, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: You are a lawyer after all, and you have certain information or knowledge about the constitutional system of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If Serbs were to walk out and had not taken part in this voting, would, according to you, the vote conducted by the Croats and the Muslims be something that constituted the violation of the rights of Serbs as a constituent people of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Still, if I were to tell you, because I did study these matters quite a lot, that the vital interests of Serbs were really, truly violated, would you not confirm that assertion?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That is what you state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do state that. So please, could you change your position? Would you agree to change your position if I were to tell you that on the basis of these principles there was a violation of the vital interests of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you are trying to make me go the way you want. I don't know. This is your interpretation. It's not my interpretation. Still, I am giving you the answer that I don't know. Because there were loyal Serbs and deputies in Sarajevo, too, who voted for that declaration and passed it, and I'm still giving you the answer that I don't know. Don't force me to give you answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, perhaps this is a convenient point for you to break and decide how best to utilise your remaining 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I must say to the witness that your cross-examination has not yet been completed, and therefore you must return tomorrow. Now, because you are sworn as a witness in this matter, you can't speak to the attorneys from either side, nor can you discuss your testimony with anybody else. So any conversation you have with persons other than the attorneys cannot relate to the testimony that you have given here. And I remind counsel and the parties that when we resume at 2.15 testimony it will be in Courtroom II. So we take the adjournment to 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of October, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
